transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Well, nice to meet you, Doc. I appreciate you taking the time to see me. You know, it's funny, because when you work your whole life, you think stopping is going to be this big relief, right? You picture yourself sitting on the porch with a cup of coffee, maybe reading the paper, finally taking a breath. 

But what brings me in is that ever since I stopped working... I just, well, I can’t seem to slow down. At all. It's like my motor is still running on high and nobody showed me where the off switch is. I wake up early and I'm just up and moving from one little job to the next all day long. I'll start fixing a loose hinge on the kitchen cabinet, and before I even put the screwdriver away I'm out in the yard pulling weeds, and then I'm in the garage trying to reorganize the workbenches. It's just go, go, go. It honestly feels exactly like I still have a crew waiting on me to tell them what to do, you know? Like if I don't keep moving and finding tasks, the whole job site is gonna fall apart, even though it's just my house now and there's no deadline for any of it. My wife keeps telling me to just sit down in the recliner and watch a ballgame like a normal retired guy, but I just can't seem to stay put.
Since you stopped working, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling unusually happy, energetic, or excited about things? Or has your mood stayed pretty much the same?

Happy? Excited? No, Doc, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, it's not like I'm walking around throwing a parade every day just because I don't have to punch a clock anymore. My mood is... well, it's pretty much just regular old me, you know? 

I mean, sure, I'm glad I don't have to deal with the site managers breathing down my neck anymore, or waking up at 4:30 in the morning to scrape ice off the truck windshield in the dead of February. That part is definitely a relief. But I'm not walking around on cloud nine or feeling some kind of big thrill about things. If anything, I get a little aggravated with myself sometimes because I can't just settle down and enjoy the peace and quiet. 

Like just last Tuesday, I was trying to watch this documentary on the History Channel—it was about the Pacific theater in World War II, really interesting stuff, my dad served in the Navy on a destroyer so I always try to watch those when they come on—and I was in a perfectly fine mood, just normal, but I still ended up pausing the TV four different times. First because I remembered the gutters needed clearing, and then on the way out to the garage I saw a spot on the hallway carpet that needed scrubbing, and before I knew it I was reorganizing the hall closet. 

So, no, I'm not unusually happy or giddy or fired up about life or anything like that. My mood is exactly the same as it's been for forty years. The energy is just... it's all physical, in my hands and my feet, I guess you could say, not in my mood. Does that make sense? I'm just regular, just can't seem to sit still.

You mentioned your energy and restlessness started when you stopped working. Before you retired, when you were working all those years, were you able to sit down and relax without feeling this constant need to be moving and doing things?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because looking back on it now, I guess... well, I guess the short answer is no, not really. But it was different back then, Doc. See, when I was working, I was a general contractor for thirty-eight years. Thirty-eight years! And when you're running a job site, you don't sit down. You just don't. You're always walking the site, checking the framing, making sure the electricians aren't getting in the way of the plumbers, dealing with inspectors... it's a twelve-hour day on your feet, easy. 

So when I was working, that restlessness, that constant need to go, go, go—it was just called being good at my job. People praised me for it. They'd say, "Oh, Frank, he's a machine, he never stops, he gets it done." And then I'd get home, usually around six or seven, and I'd be so dog-tired from being on my feet all day that I'd eat dinner and fall asleep in the chair by eight-thirty. I didn't have the energy to be restless at home because I left it all at the job site.

But even then, on the weekends... man, my wife used to get so mad at me. Sunday was supposed to be our day of rest, right? We'd go to early service at the church, come home, and she'd want to just read a book or watch a movie. And I'd try, I really would. I'd sit on the couch with her for maybe ten, fifteen minutes, but then my leg would start bouncing. Just bouncing up and down like a jackhammer. And then I'd start thinking about the lawn mower needing a new spark plug, or the gutters needing cleaning, or maybe I should go down to the hardware store just to look at the new power tools. Next thing you know, I'm out in the garage for six hours on a Sunday afternoon. 

So I guess, no, I've never really been able to just sit and relax. It's just that before, I had a place to put all that energy, a place where it made sense and paid the bills. Now that I'm retired, it's like... it's like all that energy is still there, but it doesn't have anywhere to go, so it's just bouncing around inside my house, driving me and my wife crazy. Does that make sense? I mean, I always thought it was just my work ethic, but now that there's no work, it's still happening.

Going back to when you were a kid in school—did your teachers ever say you had trouble sitting still in class, or did your parents notice you were always on the go even back then? Or was this constant restlessness something that really started when you began working?

Well, you're taking me way back now, Doc. Way back. I mean, we're talking about the early sixties here, back when I was at Thomas Jefferson Elementary. And, well, to tell you the truth, it was exactly the same back then. I guess I’ve always had this motor running. My mom, God rest her soul, she used to say I came out of the womb ready to frame a house.

But in school... yeah, it was a real problem for the teachers. Even back in grade school, my teachers would always tell my parents at those parent-teacher conferences—I remember my mom coming home and sighing, sitting down at the kitchen table—they'd say I was a really bright kid, but I was just completely scattered. That was the word they always used. Scattered. 

I mean, I could never keep track of my things. I was always, and I mean always, losing my pencils. My dad used to joke that I must be eating them because he was buying a new pack of those yellow number two pencils every single week for me. I'd leave them in the cafeteria, drop them on the bus, chew the erasers off... who knows where they went. 

And I just couldn't keep my mouth shut, either. If the teacher asked a question and I knew the answer, I wouldn't bother raising my hand or waiting my turn. I'd just blurt it right out. Call out the answer before anyone else even had a chance to think. It drove Mrs. Higgins in the third grade absolutely up the wall. She used to make me go clap the chalk erasers outside just to get me out of the room for five minutes.

And sitting still to do the actual work? Forget about it. The only thing I cared about was recess, getting outside to play kickball or just run around on the blacktop and burn off some of that energy. But I'd get so distracted looking out the window or messing with the hinges on my desk that I wouldn't do my assignments. The teachers were constantly having to come over, tap on my paper, and give me reminders that I had to actually finish my work before I was allowed to go out for recess. If they didn't stand right there and remind me, it just wouldn't get done. I'd be drawing trucks or taking apart my pen instead.

So, yeah, long story short, it definitely didn't start when I began working. It was there right from the get-go. It's just that once I got older and got into construction, nobody cared if I was calling out or moving around—they actually paid me for it! But sitting in a little wooden desk in a classroom? Oh, it was torture, Doc. Absolute torture.
